evidence_context.text: OrbitVitals summary of the NASA web page "Science in Space: Week of Sept. 15, 2023 - Sleep on Station" (section "Science in Space: Week of Sept. 15, 2023 - Sleep on Station"): In the Sleep In Orbit investigation, each astronaut's natural sleep on Earth is recorded before and after the mission to form an individual baseline, and sleep recorded on the space station is then compared with that baseline.

OrbitVitals summary of the NASA web page "Science in Space: Week of Sept. 15, 2023 - Sleep on Station" (section "Science in Space: Week of Sept. 15, 2023 - Sleep on Station"): The Sleep-Long experiment found that scheduled sleep was out of step with the body clock in roughly one of every five sleep episodes on the station. In those episodes crew members slept nearly one hour less and rated their sleep as poorer, and misalignment was more likely in periods of critical operations, for example while a vehicle was docked.

OrbitVitals summary of the peer-reviewed article "On-orbit sleep problems of astronauts and countermeasures" (Wu B et al., Military Medical Research, 2018; section "Design reasonable on-orbit work-rest schedules"): Work-rest schedules for a mission are planned before flight around launch and landing times, crew size, time-critical events, workload, mission objectives and shift pattern. The review adds that the schedule should include interesting work and enough time for rest and recreation so that fatigue does not become sustained.

interpretations.text: The configured screen flagged sleep_duration for review (configured pattern: progressive_duration_reduction). This is a statistical pattern in the recorded values relative to the crew member's own baseline. It asks a person to look at the data; it does not establish a cause or a health condition.
No configured signal was found for sleep_efficiency in the usable records. This means the screen did not trigger; it does not show that the crew member is well.

uncertainties.text: Some nights in the window have no usable record. The reason is unknown, and a missing night is not evidence of poor or good sleep.
'attention' is produced by screening settings chosen for this demonstration. They are not clinical thresholds, and the screen is not a statistical significance test.
All crew data in this explanation is simulated. It shows how the software behaves, not how a person responds to spaceflight.
The cited summaries of published sources are general context about spaceflight. They do not describe this crew member and do not validate the screening settings.
